TRUMP PRAISES HALEY STEVENS: Democrat's 'BRAVERY' Backing Rogers Over El-Sayed
sources.text:
President Donald Trump praised Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI) on Sunday after the congresswoman announced she is backing Republican Mike Rogers over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan's U.S. Senate race, calling her decision an act of bravery and a major development in one of the country's most closely watched contests.
"Wow, this is BIG!"
The president's praise followed Stevens' video announcement posted to X, in which she said El-Sayed had made clear she was no longer welcome in his campaign.
"Hey Michigan, as you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away. And he's right. And that's why I'm endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today," Stevens said.
Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in Michigan's August Democratic primary, described herself as "a very proud Democrat" who loves her state but said she could not support El-Sayed, citing his backing from political streamer Hasan Piker, according to Fox News. She had pressed El-Sayed to condemn an outside group's ad linking U.S. support for Israel to higher grocery prices, which she called antisemitic.
The endorsement came after Stevens was disinvited from a planned church event with El-Sayed at Detroit's Perfecting Church. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-MI), who helped organize the appearance, said Stevens was asked to skip it after the dispute became a distraction and upset the church's bishop. Stevens instead appeared at the church alongside Rogers, and then released her video.
Rogers, appearing outside the church, told reporters he was honored by the support. "This is more a statement about standing together against hate and the future of this state and this country than it is anything else," he said.
The endorsement drew immediate backlash from Democrats, according to The Guardian, which reported that some of Stevens' own campaign staff quit following the announcement. CNN correspondent Manu Raju reported that longtime chief of staff Justin German and communications director Logan Basch were among those who left.
El-Sayed, speaking at a rally on Sunday — the same event Stevens had been disinvited from — told reporters he does not think about his former primary rival. "At the end of the day, I actually don't think about Haley Stevens," he said, adding that voters who oppose hate should not support Rogers, Trump and Vice President JD Vance.
Trump's post marked a striking turn: Stevens' website reportedly includes an entire page dedicated to denouncing his policies, according to The Guardian.
The Michigan Senate race is one of the most competitive in the country and could determine which party controls the Senate. El-Sayed defeated Stevens by a narrow margin in August, and she had for months declined to openly campaign for him.
ABC News noted the president's praise in a post on X, writing: "President Trump lavished praise on Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan after she endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the Senate race, who defeated Stevens in the primary."
Our Take
For once, a Democrat put principle over party — and the president noticed. Haley Stevens looked at Abdul El-Sayed's refusal to condemn antisemitic rhetoric from his supporters, his embrace by a streamer with a history of inflammatory commentary, and she said: enough. That took guts, and Trump is right to call it out.
Notice what the Democrats did in response. They didn't debate her arguments. They called it a "betrayal" and her own staff walked out. That tells you everything about the modern Left: there's no room for dissent, no room for a Democrat who thinks for herself, and no room for anyone who won't fall in line behind a nominee whose campaign has been dogged by questions about antisemitism.
El-Sayed's response — "I actually don't think about Haley Stevens" — is the tell. He doesn't think about the voters she represents, either. He's running for a Senate seat in a state where the Jewish community and its allies are watching closely, and he won't answer the simplest question about hate in his own coalition.
Patriots should be paying attention to Michigan. This race is a test of whether common sense can beat party loyalty, and Stevens just cast her vote for common sense. The question now is whether Michigan voters will do the same on Election Day.

“A manic apotheosis of mutual dorkdom:” the ballad of the flakiest ratfucker
Haley Stevens’s Pierre Laval moment is obviously reprehensible, but it’s also bizarre even by the standards of this creepy weirdo. I can’t recall anything comparable to a primary loser doing a last-minute endorsement of their opponent while still telling people she wasn’t going to do that. According to Josh Marshall, her staff was still expecting her to campaign with the Democratic nominee this morning:
Let me share a few quick thoughts about former Democratic Senate primary candidate Haley Stevens. As you’ve likely seen, Stevens showed up this morning at a Black church in Detroit with Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers. Let me say first that my best guess is that Abdul El-Sayed is going to win this race and that all this final-days drama with Stevens won’t end up to have mattered. I will also say that I can’t remember a spectacle quite like this, or any defeated Democratic primary candidate crashing out like this, in 30-plus years of observing Democratic politics very, very closely.
On Friday I said that while to that point I’d questioned Stevens’ judgment, wisdom and decision-making, I was now questioning her sanity. That was only slightly tongue-in-cheek. And even less so now. There’s a level of erratic, boffo behavior here that is even more than appears on the surface. From a mix of watching the morning shows and my own reporting, I can tell you that as recently as last night Stevens told multiple Democratic power players that she was still going to vote for Abdul El-Sayed. Last night. As I’m writing this, in addition to the church appearance, I’ve just seen that she is now officially endorsing Mike Rogers. She seems to be blaming that to some degree on that fact that she was disinvited from today’s Democratic unity rally. But whatever you think of Stevens and El-Sayed, her statement in advance of that rally made disinviting her unavoidable. She quite literally forced it.
I don’t know Stevens, have never met her, though I know a number of people who do know her quite well. At least from the outside, and to some degree from the inside, it does appear that there is some sort of mutual catalyzing and mutual weirdness-escalation between Stevens and her fiancé, Jason Turkish, who caused headlines last week by announcing that he planned to vote for Mike Rogers. Watching their tag-teaming over the last few days, there’s a vibe of two dorky high schoolers who find true love and then launch into some kind of manic apotheosis of mutual dorkdom. Everyone deserves happiness and to find their soulmate, obviously. But it’s quite a thing to see unfolding like this at the center of a top-tier Senate campaign.
Each thing that has happened over the last 36 hours seem to have been a total surprise, even to her closest aides and advisors; as the Detroit News is apparently now reporting, all or most of her senior House staff resigned this morning. Staff was literally waiting for her at this morning’s Clyburn unity event thinking she was about to arrive.
I also endorse JMM’s supplemental commentary:
My recent comments about how there’s no viable alternative to respecting the decision of primary voters in a large brokerage party apply even more forcefully to the candidates participating in these primaries. Earlier this summer Stevens was seeking to represent Democratic voters in a critical Senate race, and she’s now endorsing a standard-issue MAGA Republican out of pure personal spite. Whatever vitriol she receives from this it’s not nearly enough.
And to state the obvious, Schumer putting the resources of the party behind this dipshit instead of McMorrow or El-Sayed is yet another reason why it’s pretty clearly time for him to go.
…I also think this is probably correct:
It’s unclear that any of this will ultimately affect voter sentiment. At least one Democratic donor was skeptical there was any reason to be concerned.
“No. She couldn’t move votes for herself,” the donor said, in reference to her failed primary run against El-Sayed.
…it is gratifying how quickly Stevens has been disowned by every faction of the party:
"Stevens was also removed from a series of House Democratic member text chats Sunday, according to three of the people, who were granted anonymity to speak candidly."

Democrats turn on each other in Michigan ahead of midterm elections
Detroit — Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the US Senate primary, Haley Stevens, has stunned party officials by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers as Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill.
Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary.
“Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. “And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.”
El-Sayed dismissed the endorsement when asked about it by reporters later on Sunday, saying he’s focused on issues voters care about, such as the high cost of living.
“At the end of the day I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he said, adding later: “None of this matters.”
Michigan Democratic leaders were left shocked. With just less than 48 hours to go before Election Day, a party that had spent months trying to unite behind its Senate nominee was suddenly grappling with an extraordinary defection in one of this year’s most important races.
Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the US ally. He has also been criticised by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker.
El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is facing Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by the retiring Democrat, Gary Peters. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party’s effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump’s second term.
Stevens and El-Sayed were originally scheduled to attend church together, along with other Michigan and national Democrats, including South Carolina representative Jim Clyburn. Democrats hoped it would be a show of unity as they worked to boost turnout in the Detroit area, where concerns have lingered about enthusiasm among Black and Jewish voters in key Democratic strongholds.
Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded.
After the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and her fiancé Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, “I’m not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote.”
Rogers, standing beside her, said he was “honoured” by her support.

sources.news_title: Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers called a ‘disgrace’ at Detroit unity roundtable
sources.text:
Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers called a ‘disgrace’ at Detroit unity roundtable
The roundtable came hours after Stevens withdrew her support for El-Sayed and endorsed his Republican opponent, drawing condemnation from Democrats.
Supporters of Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed gather for a roundtable of Black, Arab and Muslim Michiganders in Detroit on Nov. 1, 2026. (Photo by Minnah Arshad/Michigan Advance)
Organizers with the Abdul El-Sayed campaign hosted a conversation with Black, Arab and Muslim Americans in Detroit on Sunday afternoon in an effort to unify Democrats in the final stretch before the election.
Former U.S. Rep. Jamaal Bowman of New York, state Senate candidate Abbas Alawieh, Michigan United organizer Elder Leslie Matthews and Uncommitted co-founder Layla Elabed were among the speakers on Sunday afternoon.
The invite-only roundtable, moderated by the Women for Abdul coalition and Reproductive Freedom for All Michigan, drew about two dozen people to Haraz Coffee House, a Yemeni cafe in Detroit. It began shortly after U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham) withdrew her support for El-Sayed and endorsed Republican nominee Mike Rogers in an 11th-hour announcement that drew widespread condemnation from Democratic Party leaders.
Bowman, who represented New York’s 16th Congressional District until last year, called Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers a “disgrace” and said she “represents white supremacy.”
“This is a reckoning of American democracy. Haley Stevens showed you who she was,” he said. “We can never let white supremacy win. When there is division or hate, it’s rooted in that.”
Bowman added that voters can never forget what Stevens did.
“The more they keep us believing that we are separate, that we are different, the more they create the economic and social conditions that we are crabs in a barrel fighting to get over each other in lieu of the other, and if we internalize those beliefs, that is the thing that makes us weak,” Bowman said.
In the August primary, Stevens performed strongly among Black voters, including in Detroit, where she defeated El-Sayed by 28 percentage points. Her campaign and its supporters, including AIPAC’s super PAC, ran ads tailored to Black voters. The ads had criticized El-Sayed’s support for the Uncommitted movement in the 2024 presidential primary, which was a protest movement over the Biden administration’s handling of Gaza. El-Sayed later endorsed Kamala Harris for president the day after she announced her campaign.
Since then, El-Sayed has sought to win over Black voters in Detroit and across the state, as polls suggest a tight race on Tuesday. El-Sayed will likely need strong turnout among Black Michiganders, a reliably Democratic voting bloc, to defeat Rogers.
Word of Stevens’ defection has drawn widespread condemnation from all wings of the Democratic Party. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-New York), who back Stevens during the primary, called her decision a “despicable betrayal,” while Democratic National Committee Black Caucus Chair Virgie Rollins said Stevens had “revealed herself to be a sellout who used Black Michiganders for a political stunt.”
This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens.
Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors.
— Chuck Schumer (@chuckschumer) November 1, 2026
Alawieh, who cross-endorsed El-Sayed, said at the event on Sunday that he has benefited from “a world where my parents had their full rights, where they had access to economic opportunity,” which he said would not have been possible without the generational sacrifices of Black Americans. He called out anti-Black racism among Arab Americans, including stereotypes he heard as a child that “Black neighborhoods are somehow inherently dangerous.”
“There is pain between our communities from where we come from,” he said. “If we’re honest about where the hurt has been, then we can take that next step forward and that next one after that,” Alawieh said.
Alawieh also said he’s supporting El-Sayed not “because he looks like me,” but because of the Senate nominee’s policies.
“What our communities know more than anyone, and many Black women have taught us this more than anyone, is you don’t need to vote for someone who looks exactly like you in order for your interests to be represented,” Alawieh said. “If the interests of women would be represented best by only a woman candidate, then we would not be living in a world where Haley Stevens so quickly sells out the right to choose, sells out voting rights, sells out health care, just so she can go support a genocide-enabling Mike Rogers.”
Elder Leslie Mathews, an organizer with Michigan United, said at the event that she had built relationships with Arab American and Palestinian women in the last three years in her anti-war advocacy for Gaza. Matthews said she was attending the discussion in her personal capacity.
“It’s not even about being Black and Arab, but it’s really about being human,” Mathews said.
Mathews spoke about the frustration and pain she felt in 2024 over the presidential election, when some Arab Americans, Muslims, and pro-Palestinian supporters declined to back former Vice President Kamala Harris for president over Gaza.
“One of the reasons why we lost that election was because we didn’t come together, because I felt that you couldn’t feel my pain, you felt that I couldn’t feel your pain,” Mathews said.
Now, Mathews said she hopes to unify Black and brown communities behind a united agenda, and said El-Sayed is “one of the things that we can all fight for.”
Layla Elabed, who co-founded the 2024 Uncommitted movement to protest the Biden administration’s handling of Gaza, said Black and brown women are often celebrated as the backbone of democracy “while keeping us out of the places where decisions are made.”
“There is a history of Black communities being told that they cannot govern themselves. We experienced this firsthand in Detroit under emergency management,” she said. “These experiences, the lessons I learned, especially as somebody born and raised in Detroit, sometimes the very people who tell you how important your voice is becomes uncomfortable the moment you decide to use it.”

DETROIT (AP) — Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers as Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill.
Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary.
“Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. “And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.”
El-Sayed dismissed the endorsement when asked about it by reporters later Sunday, saying he’s focused on issues voters care about, such as the high cost of living.
“At the end of the day I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he said, adding later: “None of this matters.”
Michigan Democratic leaders were left shocked. With just less than 48 hours to go before Election Day, a party that had spent months trying to unite behind its Senate nominee was suddenly grappling with an extraordinary defection in one of this year’s most important races.
Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. He has also been criticized by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker.
El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is facing Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by the retiring Democrat, Gary Peters. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party’s effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump’s second term.
Stevens and El-Sayed were originally scheduled to attend church together, along with other Michigan and national Democrats, including South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. Democrats hoped it would be a show of unity as they worked to boost turnout in the Detroit area, where concerns have lingered about enthusiasm among Black and Jewish voters in key Democratic strongholds.
Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded.
Stevens’ team resigns as Democrats are stunned by reversal
After the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and her fiance Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, “I’m not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote.”
Rogers, standing beside her, said he was “honored” by her support.
Their appearance came days after Stevens publicly reaffirmed she would vote for her party’s nominee. It also led her longtime chief of staff to resign, with a number of staff members expected to follow soon, according to a person familiar with the developments who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters.
“We are shocked and heartbroken,” the aide said in a statement.
The state party chair, Curtis Hertel, said Stevens’ endorsement “shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about.”
“We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum,” Hertel wrote, and won’t let such 11th-hour “distractions” deter the campaign. Hertel later wrote that Stevens “is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.”
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, who supported Stevens in the primary, denounced her endorsement of Rogers.
“This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens,” Schumer wrote in a social media post.
Dingell says she disinvited Stevens after it became ‘distracting’
Among the Democrats who joined El-Sayed at church Sunday morning were U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan, U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Senate primary before voting began.
Dingell, a senior Democratic figure in the state who helped organize the planned joint appearance, said she asked Stevens not to attend and that Stevens told her she would abide by that.
“I’m the one who pulled it, because it had become way too distracting,” Dingell said in an interview before Stevens appeared with Rogers. “This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank.”
In the August primary, Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighboring Oakland County, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters who are important parts of the Democratic coalition.
Early voting for Tuesday’s election has been underway since Oct. 24. As of Friday, more than 1.8 million people had already voted in Michigan.
How did we get here?
The Democratic primary was among the most bitter this year. Each candidate accused the other of making personal attacks. Tens of millions of dollars in outside spending poured into the race, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s affiliated super PAC, which backed Stevens. El-Sayed took particular offense to an outside group’s ad accusing him of disrespecting women.
Although Stevens pledged after the primary to help El-Sayed however she could, the two have not appeared together publicly since a unity breakfast two days after his primary win.
Last week Stevens’ fiance told The Detroit News that he would vote for Rogers. Stevens later appeared on CNN to reaffirm her support for El-Sayed but urged his campaign to “shut out the hate and call it out.”
But on Friday, after The Associated Press reported on the planned joint appearance, Stevens released a lengthy statement calling on El-Sayed to condemn an ad by an independent left-wing group that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices.
“Abdul promises to get money out of politics,” Stevens wrote. “He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.”
El-Sayed responded: “So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand.”
He made clear the ad was not made by his campaign and said “I do not agree with the contents of that ad.”
Trump and Republicans revel in the discord
Trump praised Stevens in a Truth Social post, saying she was “a Highly Respected Democrat” and that her support from Black and Jewish voters in Michigan is “virtually unprecedented.”
“Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did,” Trump wrote. “It’s a thing called bravery, and few people have it like just displayed by Congresswoman Haley Stevens!”
Appearing with Trump in Iowa for a campaign rally, House Speaker Mike Johnson said that he spoke to Stevens after she endorsed Rogers. Johnson said he “encouraged her to stay safe and keep speaking the truth.”
A spokesman for the Republican National Committee, Hunter Lovell, said Democrats who feel abandoned by El-Sayed “have a home” with Rogers.

'This is BIG': Trump praises Haley Stevens after she backs Republican Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan Senate race
President Trump has praised Democrat Haley Stevens on Truth Social, calling her endorsement of Mike Rogers for the Michigan Senate seat.
President Donald Trump has praised Democrat Haley Stevens after she broke with her party to endorse Republican Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race. Her surprise move has sparked a political stir just days before the midterm elections, especially after her public fallout with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
What Trump wrote
“Wow, this is BIG! Congresswoman Haley Stevens, a Highly Respected Democrat, who narrowly lost in the Primary to Abdul Mohamed El-Sayed, and who has been breathlessly wined and dined by the Dumocrats to help in their Michigan Campaign for the United States Senate against Mike Rogers, has just ENDORSED Mike Rogers for Senate!” Trump wrote on his Truth Social post.
“Her following is huge, and the level of respect from the People of Michigan, especially our African American and Jewish populations, is virtually unparalleled. Haley said what few people are willing to say,” he continued.
Trump added that Stevens “showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did.” He ended with: “It’s a thing called bravery, and few people have it like just displayed by Congresswoman Haley Stevens!"
Why Stevens backed Rogers
Haley Stevens is a Democratic member of the US House of Representatives from Michigan.
This year, she ran in the Democratic primary for Michigan’s Senate seat and lost to Abdul El-Sayed after a tense fight. El-Sayed is now the Democratic nominee. Mike Rogers, a former Republican Representative from Michigan, is the Republican nominee.
On Sunday, just two days before the midterm elections, Stevens broke with her party and endorsed Rogers instead of El-Sayed. She also appeared with Rogers at a church in Detroit the same day, as per The Hill.
Stevens said she took this step because El-Sayed had told her to stay away. “As you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for US Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away. And he’s right, and that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today,” she said, according to CNN.
Stevens was supposed to attend a campaign event with El-Sayed, but he dropped her from it, according to The Hill. This happened after days of public and private clashes between the two. The disagreement was mainly over Israel and the war in Gaza. The issue played a major role in their primary fight, their recent feud and Stevens’ decision to back Rogers. El-Sayed wants the US to stop sending financial aid to Israel and use that money for domestic issues. During the primary, Stevens received millions of dollars from pro-Israel lobbying groups. This became a major point of disagreement between the two.
El-Sayed mostly brushed off questions about the endorsement, according to CNN. “At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he said.

sources.text:
DETROIT | Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers after Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill.
Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary.
“Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. “And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.”
El-Sayed dismissed the endorsement when asked about it by reporters later Sunday, saying he’s focused on issues voters care about, such as the high cost of living.
“At the end of the day I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he said, adding later: “None of this matters.”
Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. He has also been criticized by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker.
El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is facing Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by the retiring Democrat, Gary Peters. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party’s effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump’s second term.
Democrats had hoped Sunday would offer a show of unity as they worked to boost turnout in the Detroit area, where concerns have lingered about enthusiasm among Black and Jewish voters in key Democratic strongholds.
Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded.
Stevens’ team resigns as Democrats are stunned by reversal
Plans for Stevens to join El-Sayed and Clyburn unraveled after a dispute over Israel and an outside group’s campaign advertisement escalated into a public exchange of criticism between the rivals.
After the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and fiance Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, “I’m not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote.”
Rogers, standing beside her, said he was “honored” by her support.
Their appearance stunned Democrats, coming days after Stevens publicly reaffirmed she would vote for her party’s nominee. It also led her longtime chief of staff to resign, with a number of staff members expected to follow soon, according to a person familiar with the developments who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters.
“We are shocked and heartbroken,” the aide said in a statement.
The state party chair, Curtis Hertel, said Stevens’ endorsement “shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about.”
“We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum,” Hertel wrote, and won’t let such 11th-hour “distractions” deter the campaign. Hertel later wrote that Stevens “is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.”
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, who supported Stevens in the primary, denounced her endorsement of Rogers.
“This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens,” Schumer wrote in a social media post.
Dingell says she disinvited Stevens after it became ‘distracting’
Among the Democrats who joined El-Sayed at church Sunday morning were U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan, U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Senate primary before voting began.
Dingell, a senior Democratic figure in the state who helped organize the planned joint appearance in hopes of bringing together Democrats, said she asked Stevens not to attend and that Stevens told her she would abide by that.
“I’m the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting,” Dingell said in a telephone interview before Stevens appeared with Rogers. “This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank.”
Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighboring Oakland County, in the primary, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters who are important parts of the Democratic coalition.
Early voting has been underway since Oct. 24. As of Friday, more than 1.8 million people had already voted in Michigan. A total of 4.5 million ballots were cast in the 2022 midterm election, a record for a nonpresidential year.
How did we get here?
The Democratic primary was among the most bitter this year. Each candidate accused the other of making personal attacks. Tens of millions of dollars in outside spending poured into the race, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s affiliated super PAC, which backed Stevens. El-Sayed took particular offense to an outside group’s ad accusing him of disrespecting women.
Although Stevens pledged after the primary to help El-Sayed however she could, the two have not appeared together publicly since a unity breakfast two days after his August win.
Last week Stevens’ fiance told The Detroit News that he would vote for Rogers. Stevens later appeared on CNN to reaffirm her support for El-Sayed but urged his campaign to “shut out the hate and call it out.”
But on Friday, after The Associated Press reported on the planned joint appearance, Stevens released a lengthy statement calling on El-Sayed to condemn an ad by an independent left-wing group that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices.
“Abdul promises to get money out of politics,” Stevens wrote. “He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.”
El-Sayed responded: “So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand.”
He made clear the ad was not made by his campaign and said “I do not agree with the contents of that ad.”
Trump and Republicans revel in the discord
Trump praised Stevens in a Truth Social post, saying she was “a Highly Respected Democrat” and that her support from Black and Jewish voters in Michigan is “virtually unprecedented.”
“Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did,” Trump wrote. “It’s a thing called bravery, and few people have it like just displayed by Congresswoman Haley Stevens!”
A spokesman for the Republican National Committee, Hunter Lovell, said in a statement that Democrats who feel abandoned by El-Sayed “have a home” with Rogers.
“When Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who ran against Abdul El-Sayed and knows him better than anyone, stands with Mike Rogers, Michigan should take notice,” he said.
Cappelletti reported from Washington.

Jim Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded.
Stevens’ team resigns as Democrats are stunned by reversal
Plans for Stevens to join El-Sayed and Clyburn unraveled after a dispute over Israel and an outside group’s campaign advertisement escalated into a public exchange of criticism between the rivals.
After the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and fiance Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, “I’m not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote.”

“We are shocked and heartbroken,” the aide said in a statement.

Appearing later in a brief press conference with Rogers, she again referenced the streamer: “We can’t stand with hate. We can’t stand with Hasan Piker.”
Rogers, standing next to Stevens, invoked darker messaging when referencing the PAC ad.
“Blaming a certain group of people for your problems, that sounds like 1933,” he said. “And it has consequences for those communities. Jewish Democrats are calling me, afraid for their children to stay in the state of Michigan.”
Piker, on social media, called Stevens “a self interested striver who’s weirdly obsessed with Israel and has been paid handsomely for this strange obsession.” El-Sayed has distanced himself multiple times from Piker since they campaigned together in the primary, including this week after Piker compared a heavily Jewish Michigan suburb to “a KKK neighborhood.”
A Jewish Telegraphic Agency request for comment to the Stevens-Turkish camp was not immediately returned. Stevens, who represents a heavily Jewish district in suburban Detroit, told The New York Times this weekend that she was considering converting to Judaism for their wedding.
El-Sayed, in his own press conference Sunday, dismissed Stevens’ move and preemptively warned reporters not to ask him about it. “At the end of the day I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he said.
He did, however, push back on the idea that a Rogers endorsement was standing against hate.
“If you are somebody who believes that we should stand up to hate, and you have watched this last campaign, I think we probably would not want to support Mike Rogers and Donald Trump and JD Vance,” he said. The GOP’s messaging against El-Sayed has been criticized for leaning heavily into stoking fears about Islam.
Stevens insisted she was “still a very proud Democrat.” Yet many of her staff, including her chief of staff, resigned en masse following her move Sunday. Arik Wolk, Stevens’ former campaign spokesperson, wrote on X that her endorsement was “ridiculous and pathetic.”
Some Jewish Democrats also heavily criticized Stevens on Sunday, saying she was hurting the party and the country. “Anyone who makes an election this important about themselves, and not Michiganders and our democracy, should think hard about whether they are serving the greater good,” moderate Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who is Jewish and who has hit the campaign trail with El-Sayed, wrote on X.
J Street, the liberal pro-Israel lobby that did not endorse El-Sayed, said Stevens was “weaponizing real fears about rising antisemitism to further her own grievances.”
The Jewish Democratic Council of America, an organizing body for Jewish interests in the Democratic Party, had pointedly not endorsed El-Sayed during the campaign. Yet following Stevens’ announcement, its CEO Halie Soifer wrote, “A vote for any Republican in 2026 is a vote for Donald Trump.”

Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials on Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in the general election contest after Democratic tensions boiled over. The move came after Stevens was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed as he campaigned for the Michigan seat. The outcome could help determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill.
President Donald Trump is closing out the final days of a turbulent midterm campaign with rallies in Iowa and Kansas, two states he has handily won in the past, underscoring the defensive posture his Republican Party is taking as the elections become a referendum on his second term.
A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses. Revelations came last week from The New York Times that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher who shares the incumbent’s name, to join the Senate race in Alaska.
The Latest:
Hundreds of Trump supporters gather in a festive atmosphere for his Kansas rally
President Trump was trying to boost Kansas Republican Sen. Roger Marshall’s reelection campaign in a tight race that has become the most expensive contest in Kansas history.
The outdoor rally was planned for later Sunday at the airport in Salina, about 110 miles west of Topeka, a venue seating at least 2,000 people.
Methodist megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton is bidding to become the first Democratic candidate in Kansas to win a Senate race in 94 years. Democrats have poured $62 million into television and digital ads, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.
Marshall and Republican groups have spent $43 million, bringing total ad spending to $105 million.
Trump supporters are waiting in Kansas for his next rally
Among those waiting for President Donald Trump at his later rally in Kansas was Liz Wagner, a 59-year-old restaurant owner.
She traveled from Atchison, Kansas, on the state’s eastern border, to attend Trump’s planned outdoor rally later Sunday at the airport in Salina, Kansas.
“I want people to get up and go to work and stop sticking their hands out,” she said while waiting to get into the rally. “The Democrats like to hand things out.”
She plans to vote on Election Day for Republican incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall, who’s running against Democrat Adam Hamilton.
Luke Aines, a roofing company operator in western Kansas, also was on hand with his three teenage daughters and spoke of voting a straight Republican ticket.
He said he supports banning transgender girls and women from female sports teams, as a Kansas law does. Two of his daughters compete in rodeo, and his third daughter is a wrestler. “They only wrestle girls, which I’m grateful for,” he said. “We wouldn’t be doing it, otherwise.”
In Iowa, Trump continues his commentary on Republicans’ appearances
President Donald Trump continued his commentary on the appearance of Republican candidates, this time saying Iowa’s GOP Senate candidate, Ashley Hinson, “put herself in shape” without using GLP-1 drugs.
“I knew Ashley for a long time, and she was a little bit heavier,” Trump said. “She knew what she was doing, she knew the weight that was on her. Really, literally the weight, and she knew the importance of what she was doing. And she went out — the old fashioned way too, not with ‘give me a shot.’”
After being interrupted by a protester, he continued.
“She went on a regimen, she put herself in shape,” Trump said. “She’s in perfect shape. She was great the other way. But she put herself in shape and she did that for you.”
He contrasted her weight loss with his own experience, saying, “Me, I put on a couple of pounds.”
Trump says he’d love for Haley Stevens to switch parties
President Donald Trump told rallygoers in Iowa that Democrat Haley Stevens “was very brave” to cross the aisle and endorse a Republican in Michigan’s Senate race.
“I don’t know Haley. I’ve never met Haley. But Haley said what few people were willing to say,” Trump said Sunday. “I’d love her to join the Republican Party actually.”
Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Stevens, stunned party officials by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers. The development came as Democratic tensions have boiled over days before the midterm election concludes Tuesday.
The president was speaking at the first of two rallies he has planned for Sunday, with another organized later in the day in Kansas.
“I love Iowa,” he said in Dubuque. He said he watched the Iowa Hawkeyes win their football game on Saturday and predicted “we’re going to have a much bigger win on Tuesday.”
Top Democrats in Congress rally in support of El-Sayed in Senate race in Michigan
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and congressional caucus leaders are standing with their party’s nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, after fellow Democrat Stevens stunned colleagues with her surprise support for Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan.
“Let’s be clear about one thing,” Jeffries said in a post. “Dr. Abdul El-Sayed will always put the American people first,” he said. He called Rogers “a partisan hack who represents more of the same MAGA extremism.”
Democratic Rep. Pramila Jayapal, of Washington state, a former leader of the progressive caucus, implored Michiganders to “stay focused on the race at hand, and cast their ballots” for El-Sayed.
“Michigan’s Senate seat will help decide whether Congress finally puts a check on Donald Trump’s overreach,” said Democratic Rep. Linda Sanchez of California, chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus’ pac. She said El-Sayed has the PAC’s “full support.”
Meanwhile, Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson said he spoke to Stevens after she endorsed Rogers.
“I’ve spoken to her, encouraged her to stay safe and keep speaking the truth and I think she’s doing that very well,” Johnson said as he and President Donald Trump arrived in Iowa for a campaign rally.
“She’s always been very thoughtful,” he said of the Democrat. “She loves her state. She served it as best she could and she’s speaking the truth.”
Democrats assail Haley Stevens over her endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers
Democrats are blistering Haley Stevens after her endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race.
Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi said Stevens had “dangerously chosen to betray” Michigan families by backing Rogers over his Senate opponent, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. El-Sayed defeated Stevens for the nomination in their party’s primary earlier this year.
Pennsylvania Rep. Susan Wild, who had been Stevens’ roommate in 2023, said she’d be a “pariah among her friends.”
Justin German, who served as Stevens’ chief of staff, said in a social media post that he and many other members of her staff have resigned over the endorsement. German also said her team still supports El-Sayed.
Messages seeking comment were left with Stevens on Sunday.
Justice Department plans appeal after judge dismisses lawsuit in Alaska’s Senate race
The Justice Department has filed notice it will appeal a federal judge’s ruling dismissing its challenge to Alaska’s certification of the U.S. Senate race if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.
“Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” a department spokesperson said in a statement.
U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason wrote in an order that the relief the Trump administration is seeking is “infeasible” because many voters have already cast ballots.
Sullivan is an ally of President Donald Trump and is facing Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola in one of the country’s most closely watched Senate contests. Tuesday’s ranked-choice election also includes a candidate — a retired teacher — who shares the incumbent’s name.
The stakes are high, and the GOP worries voters will get confused and accidentally vote for the wrong Sullivan.
Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation.
Wisconsin GOP governor’s candidate makes final push for voter support
Tom Tiffany, a member of Congress the past six years, said after a rally Sunday in heavily Democratic Madison, Wisconsin, that he can “feel” the momentum of the race breaking for him.
“This is a turnout election,” he told supporters. “This is how we’re going to win this.”
Tiffany faces Democrat David Crowley as Election Day approaches.
“I can feel it out there,” Tiffany said. “People are going to turn out on Tuesday. Be part of the movement.”
Both Tiffany and Crowley are campaigning with surrogates across the state in the final two days before the election.
Tiffany was joined at the Madison stop by U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson and former Wisconsin Gov. Tommy Thompson.
Crowley is campaigning on Sunday with Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, and on Monday he will be with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.
Kansas attorney general orders a Democratic PAC to stop offering $5 gift cards to voters
Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach says in a cease-and-desist letter to the Bluestem Fund that offering anything of value in exchange for voting violates both federal and state law.
He directed the group to preserve all records and communications related to its canvassing activities. Kobach on Saturday said a voter in Wichita alerted his office to the “brazen” offer of a gift card.
The PAC’s chair, Topeka attorney L.J. Leatherman, did not immediately respond to a phone message seeking comment.
Kobach is an ally of President Donald Trump and served as vice chair of Trump’s short-lived commission on election fraud in 2017.
In September, Kobach sent a similar letter to a League of Women Voters chapter in northeast Kansas after it offered $5 gift cards to students who registered to vote. The league chapter said it was cooperating with Kobach’s inquiry and is committed to complying with all laws.
Abdul El-Sayed’s Democratic rival, Haley Stevens, endorses GOP’s Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race
Democrat Haley Stevens says she’s voting for Mike Rogers for Senate in Michigan over her former primary opponent Abdul El-Sayed.
Stevens, standing alongside Rogers, said she’d be voting for other Democrats but would not cast her ballot for El-Sayed, who defeated her in an August primary.
“It is more a statement about standing together against hate and the future of this state and this country, than it is anything else,” she said.
Rogers said he was honored to have Stevens’ vote.
Senate Democratic leader calls fellow Democrat Haley Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers ‘betrayal’
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer has denounced Haley Stevens’ endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race.
“This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens,” Schumer wrote in a social media post of the step taken by his fellow Democrat, Stevens.
Schumer, who had backed Stevens in the primary, reiterated the party’s support for Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated her in August.
Stevens announced her endorsement of Rogers earlier Sunday in the general election contest against El_Sayed. El-Sayed dismissed it, saying he’s worried about voters’ concerns, not intraparty drama.
Abdul El-Sayed dismisses Stevens’ endorsement of GOP’s Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race
Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed batted away news that his former primary opponent Haley Stevens said she’s backing Rogers in the Michigan contest.
“At the end of the day I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he said, standing alongside Democratic Rep. James Clyburn of South Carolina and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland.
He added: “Rather than focus on a distraction about who said what to whom, where they went, I’ve been consistent. I want to get money out of politics. I want to put money back in pockets. I want Medicare for all.”
His comments came shortly after his primary opponent and fellow Democrat, Haley Stevens, said she was voting for Rogers.
Stevens’ split from the party comes two days before Election Day, which will determine which party controls Congress.
Judge dismisses lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska Senate race if GOP incumbent loses
A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses.
The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the election and with early voting underway, called for an investigation into whether votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan were intended for the senator. The state said the case lacked merit and argued there would be no way to determine that without violating voter privacy.
U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason wrote in the order that the relief the United States seeks is “infeasible” because many voters have already cast their ballots. She said the cast ballots have been mixed together to the point where they cannot be matched to specific voters.
“More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified ‘investigation’ of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” she wrote.
Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after a stroke
Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut has been hospitalized after having a stroke, his office said Sunday.
Murphy, 53, was at his son’s hockey game Saturday when he began to feel numbness in his arm. He was taken to a hospital, where doctors discovered he had had a stroke.
He was transferred to Johns Hopkins.
“The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery,” according to a statement from his office.
Murphy is in his third term in the Senate. He previously served in the House for three terms.
Georgia governor candidates attend separate church services on final Sunday of campaign
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms went to her home congregation in Atlanta before voter turnout rallies later Sunday in middle Georgia as she tries to achieve something that’s never happened: a Black woman being elected governor in the U.S.
Bottoms told her fellow members at Ben Hill United Methodist Church that her mother, a member of the church, had been “aggressive” about making sure she was back in the church before Tuesday.
Bottoms says it’s the place where she was married and had her children baptized, telling the congregation from the pulpit that the church is “always home.”
Meanwhile, Republican Rick Jackson dropped in at the north Georgia evangelical megachurch led by one of Trump’s spiritual advisers, Pastor Jentezen Franklin. Jackson did not speak at Free Chapel church in Gainesville but stood and waved as Franklin gave him an effusive welcome.
Georgia’s early vote totals please Democrats, leave Republicans nervous
Some 2.8 million early ballots were cast in Georgia, and that’s a midterm election record.
Democrats are encouraged because almost a third of the early ballots were cast by Black voters, several percentage points more than in previous elections. Latino turnout, a small slice of Georgia’s electorate, also is higher. The early electorate is also several points less white than in 2024, when Trump carried the state, and 2022, when Republican Gov. Brian Kemp was reelected.
Georgia’s metro areas, which lean Democratic, also have posted higher early turnout compared to the 2022 midterms, while most rural counties, which skew Republican, are down.
And analyses show the early vote uptick is not strictly from usual Election Day voters shifting to early ballots.
It’s enough that Kemp has cut social media videos urging Republicans to vote Tuesday and reminding them that he first won in 2018 by less than 55,000 votes, or 1.4 percentage points.
Trump supporters at Iowa rally await the president’s arrival
Dubuque, Iowa, resident Jon Lutz watches videos of President Donald Trump all the time. But Sunday afternoon’s rally will be the first time Lutz sees the man in person.
The 60-year-old civil engineer plans to cast his ballot Tuesday and said he’s a straight-ticket Republican voter.
Lutz said Trump has already accomplished so much in the first two years of his second term, and he wants to see Republicans keep control of both the House and Senate to allow his agenda to continue.
“He’s done what he’s said he’s going to do,” Lutz said. “I want him to keep going.”
Veterinarian Wendy Kuenzler, a 44-year-old from Burlington, Iowa, voted on Saturday. On Sunday she was in the concessions line at a packed arena in Dubuque, Iowa, waiting for the start of Sunday’s rally and her first time seeing Trump in person.
Kuenzler said she felt like Iowa was at a crossroads in this competitive midterm election. In the race for U.S. Senate, Kuenzler said there was no question she was supporting Republican Ashley Hinson.

Barack Obama endorses Charles Booker in race for Kentucky Senate seat
Former President Barack Obama has endorsed Charles Booker for the Kentucky U.S. Senate seat opened up by Republican Mitch McConnell’s retirement.
The two-term Democratic president said Sunday that Booker would stand up for working families.
“I’m proud to support Charles Booker for the U.S. Senate,” Obama said in a statement. “Charles cares deeply about the people of Kentucky.”
Booker, a former state legislator, is running against Republican Rep. Andy Barr.
McConnell, the former Republican leader in the Senate, is retiring after seven terms in the Senate.

Even moderate liberal commentators who had preferred Stevens over El-Sayed in the primary are furious with her. Neera Tanden, a Democratic consultant who often feuds with the left-wing of her party, accused Stevens of betraying "all of her supporters." Activist David Hogg wrote that everyone who had backed Stevens over El-Sayed should apologize and condemn her. Commentator Matthew Yglesias wrote that he was very mad at Stevens.
This strikes me as a bit much, to be honest.
Yes, it matters a great deal which party controls the Senate, and thus individual races have extremely high stakes. Pro-Trump Americans want Republican majorities to protect them from bad Democratic policies, and anti-Trump Americans want the reverse. The country's extremely defective two-party system, in which we are constantly called upon to compromise our own personal values and select the lesser of two evils, is on full display here.
But everyone slamming Stevens as some kind of traitor should know this: Unshakeable, ironclad loyalty to one's own political party is not really a virtue. I would much prefer to live under a system in which Republicans and Democrats were more likely to buck their own parties and say that supporting such and such a person is outside the bounds of what can reasonably be expected. It's encouraging that Karl Rove has refused to vote for Bo French, the nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner and an unapologetic anti-Indian racist. It would be better for the country if more Republicans followed his example—and if they similarly punished their Senate nominee, the manifestly corrupt Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
The same is true of Democrats. El-Sayed does not appear to be corrupt or racist, and some of the allegations of anti-Semitism leveled against him are unfair: Criticisms of the government of Israel are not synonymous with attacks on Jewish people. That said, he is an extremely far-left political candidate—a socialist in all but name—who thought it was a good idea to campaign with Piker, a communist sympathizer with a long track record of evincing support for terrorist groups. El-Sayed previously derided President Barack Obama, who enacted an extremely progressive policy agenda, as "fairly centrist, middle-of-the-road." Democratic primary voters are free to pick leftists to be their candidates, but normal Democrats should not feel bound by those choices. Socialism, even socialism-lite, should always be viewed as a bridge too far, because it is a ruinous ideology that produces poverty and authoritarianism.
Now it's true that Stevens appears to be doing this largely for reasons of personal spite rather than some ideological opposition to his economic agenda, so I wouldn't exactly nominate her for a Profiles in Courage Award. But the tendency to lash out at political figures who exercise a degree of independence and brand them as traitors is melodramatic at best.
As for El-Sayed: He is running well behind the Democratic Party's gubernatorial nominee, Jocelyn Benson, which suggests that Stevens is not the only Michigan Democrat feeling uncomfortable about him. We will find out on Tuesday (or maybe Wednesday morning).

A Democratic congresswoman has announced she is supporting the Republican candidate in a key senate race.

Haley Stevens's decision has been described as a "despicable betrayal".
The Democrats' messy Michigan Senate campaign has again been marred by friendly fire, with defeated primaries candidate Haley Stevens breaking ranks and endorsing the Republican nominee in Tuesday's midterm elections.
Analysts are expecting the Democrats to perform well against Donald Trump's Republican Party in many parts of the United States during this week's votes, which could reshape the Congress.

The pair's relationship plumbed new depths at the weekend, when Mr El-Sayed announced Ms Stevens was no longer invited to join him at a church service in Detroit on Sunday, local time.

Pathetic Crybaby Haley Stevens Endorses Mike Rogers
sources.text:
If one thing's been made clear through the last decade or so of national politics, it's that there are John Fettermans hiding in plain sight throughout the Democratic Party. The latest member to don the Mantle Of The Oaf is Haley Stevens, who lost her primary race for a Senate seat to Abdul El-Sayed this summer. Now, a few days before the general election, she has endorsed El-Sayed's Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.
Stevens appeared this morning at a church service in Detroit with Rogers. While entering the venue, she stopped to tell reporters that she's in favor of investing in black-owned businesses, adding, "that’s the policy that Mike’s going to take on." She then sat in the same row as Rogers during the service.
Shortly after the church service ended, Stevens, showing a tremendous understanding of her phone's camera function, officially endorsed Rogers:
This is obviously a strange thing for a Democrat to do, particularly one that had previously endorsed El-Sayed, but it's not all that surprising given how Stevens has been conducting herself since her defeat in the primary.
Stevens mostly kept quiet after losing to El-Sayed, but the spotlight fell back on her when it was announced that she was planning to appear with El-Sayed and Democratic Congressman Jim Clyburn at a church service today. Following that announcement, Stevens's fiancé, a Fetterman-flavored fellow named Jason Turkish, revealed that he would be voting for Rogers, and even went on Fox News to brag about it. Stevens then went on TV to assure people that she still planned on voting for the Democratic ticket, but then she released a spectacularly undermining statement that more or less called El-Sayed an antisemite.
Stevens's statement chided El-Sayed for not properly denouncing a political ad, made by an independent group not affiliated with his campaign, in which two people shopping for groceries complain about how expensive food has gotten while the United States gives billions of dollars of aid to Israel. Stevens, who received a staggering amount of money from pro-Israel lobbying groups during the primary, used her statement to call on El-Sayed to get "Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford." El-Sayed's campaign responded by telling Stevens that they'd actually prefer it if she just stayed away from them from now on, and that's how you end up with an ostensible Democrat, one who less than 24 hours ago was calling people within the party to ensure them she was still planning to vote for El-Sayed, endorsing a Republican in a hugely important Senate race.
It's easy to pin this hilarious and humiliating turn of events on Stevens's entanglement with the Israel lobby, and I am sure that plays a part, but this mostly reads like a person throwing a self-destructive tantrum over hurt feelings. Stevens more or less cops to this in her endorsement of Rogers, which begins with her talking about El-Sayed asking her to stay away from him. The criticisms she has attempted to level at El-Sayed's campaign are completely incoherent, and there is no useful political angle to this crack-up. Is the idea that she's going to try and remain a Democrat despite her own staff abandoning her and even the party's most dedicated centrists calling her a fool? sources.text:
Just days before Michigan’s extremely consequential Senate race, Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens switched sides ― officially endorsing Republican Mike Rogers over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday.
The Democrat told reporters on Sunday she made the endorsement decision that morning, saying she is choosing country over party.
“I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate. I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign. I do not stand with Hasan Piker, who gets trafficked on our college campuses,” Stevens said in a self-recorded video from her car. “What our students see, what our children see and who we are as Michiganders is not hate, and is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now.”
The endorsement came just after Stevens appeared at a church service with Rogers, on a day she was originally scheduled to appear at a campaign event in Detroit with El-Sayed and Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.).
“At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” El-Sayed said at his event alongside Clyburn.
“I’m just going to tell you, this is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from the government,” he told reporters. “I’m a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not the ones you guys are talking about.”
Stevens’ staff, including longtime chief of staff Justin German, resigned from her office Sunday morning. In a statement, German said staff are “shocked and heartbroken” by Stevens’ decision, and stand united to support El-Sayed.
“As of this morning, many members of our team have resigned, including myself,” German wrote. “We encourage everyone to exercise their civic duty, vote for Abdul and Democrats up and down the ballot, and stand up for the America we all believe in.”
El-Sayed’s campaign recently asked Stevens to steer clear of any remaining campaign events amid increased fracturing between the two Democrats, as Stevens became increasingly vocal against the nominee’s criticism of Israel. Clyburn stressed that Stevens was still invited to Sunday’s event at a Black church, though she made no mention of the senior Democrat at her press conference with Rogers.
Stevens’ fiancé, Jason Turkish, told The Detroit News last week he would vote for “patriot” Rogers. Rogers, with the help of the Trump administration, has run an unapologetically Islamophobic campaign against El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim senator if elected.
“Blaming a certain group of people for all of your problems? That sounds like 1933, it doesn’t sound like 1926,” Rogers said at the press conference with Stevens. “Jewish Democrats are calling me afraid for their children to stay in the state of Michigan.”
El-Sayed has repeatedly voiced his support for Michigan’s Jewish community, and last week said he is “not affiliated in any way” with a PAC that created a controversial ad depicting a couple deciding they can’t afford some grocery items after discussing how much taxpayer money goes to Israel. Stevens has said that El-Sayed did not forcefully enough condemn the ad.
“This is the conscience of the Senate right now, and our Michigan moment,” Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in the primary election, said in her video. “And I’m just letting you know where I am. I’m still a very proud Democrat, I still very much believe in everything I voted for and said, and I’ve worked really hard and will continue to do so in all the ways life’s opportunities afford.”
“Haley Stevens’ decision to campaign with Rogers ... shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about.”
But Stevens is getting no sympathy from fellow Democrats, many of whom have doubled down on their support for El-Sayed after the Michigan lawmaker’s endorsement of Rogers. Democratic National Committee chairman Ken Martin denounced the endorsement as an “effort to sow division within our party,” while Michigan Democratic Party chair Curtis Hertel said Stevens is no longer a member of the party.
“Haley Stevens’ decision to campaign with Rogers — a man who has repeatedly sold out Michigan’s working class, wants to pass a national abortion ban, and has pledged to be a loyal vote for Trump’s agenda — shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about,” Hertel said in a statement.
“We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum, and will not allow these eleventh-hour distractions [to] deter us.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) also released a statement following Stevens’ endorsement, calling the lawmaker’s move “a despicable betrayal” and saying Senate Democrats are united in their support for El-Sayed.
Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) also said the focus must be on electing Democrats like El-Sayed “up and down the ballot.”
“Michiganders are worried about how they are going to pay their mortgage and fill up their gas tanks, and the ability to afford groceries, healthcare and housing. President Donald Trump said Sunday that Stevens did what “few people are willing to say.”
“She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did,” he wrote on Truth Social. “It’s a thing called bravery, and few people have it like just displayed by Congresswoman Haley Stevens!”

sources.text:
Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers as Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill.
Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary.
“Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. “And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.”
El-Sayed dismissed the endorsement when asked about it by reporters later Sunday, saying he’s focused on issues voters care about, such as the high cost of living.
“At the end of the day I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he said, adding later: “None of this matters.”
Michigan Democratic leaders were left shocked. With just less than 48 hours to go before Election Day, a party that had spent months trying to unite behind its Senate nominee was suddenly grappling with an extraordinary defection in one of this year’s most important races.
Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. He has also been criticized by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker.
El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is facing Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by the retiring Democrat, Gary Peters. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party’s effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump’s second term.
Stevens and El-Sayed were originally scheduled to attend church together, along with other Michigan and national Democrats, including South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. Democrats hoped it would be a show of unity as they worked to boost turnout in the Detroit area, where concerns have lingered about enthusiasm among Black and Jewish voters in key Democratic strongholds.
Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded.
Abdul El-Sayed is promising universal health care, but it’s his faith Republicans are targeting
After the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and her fiancé Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, “I’m not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote.”
Rogers, standing beside her, said he was “honoured” by her support.
Their appearance came days after Stevens publicly reaffirmed she would vote for her party’s nominee. It also led her longtime chief of staff to resign, with a number of staff members expected to follow soon, according to a person familiar with the developments who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters.
“We are shocked and heartbroken,” the aide said in a statement.
The state party chair, Curtis Hertel, said Stevens’ endorsement “shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about.”
“We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum,” Hertel wrote, and won’t let such 11th-hour “distractions” deter the campaign. Hertel later wrote that Stevens “is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.”
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, who supported Stevens in the primary, denounced her endorsement of Rogers.
“This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens,” Schumer wrote in a social media post.
Among the Democrats who joined El-Sayed at church Sunday morning were U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan, U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Senate primary before voting began.
Dingell, a senior Democratic figure in the state who helped organize the planned joint appearance, said she asked Stevens not to attend and that Stevens told her she would abide by that.
“I’m the one who pulled it, because it had become way too distracting,” Dingell said in an interview before Stevens appeared with Rogers. “This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank.”
In the August primary, Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighbouring Oakland County, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters who are important parts of the Democratic coalition.
Early voting for Tuesday’s election has been under way since Oct. 24. As of Friday, more than 1.8 million people had already voted in Michigan.
Trump administration’s bid to block election certification in Alaska thrown out by judge
The Democratic primary was among the most bitter this year. Each candidate accused the other of making personal attacks. Tens of millions of dollars in outside spending poured into the race, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s affiliated super PAC, which backed Stevens. El-Sayed took particular offence to an outside group’s ad accusing him of disrespecting women.
Although Stevens pledged after the primary to help El-Sayed however she could, the two have not appeared together publicly since a unity breakfast two days after his primary win.
Last week Stevens’ fiancé told The Detroit News that he would vote for Rogers. Stevens later appeared on CNN to reaffirm her support for El-Sayed but urged his campaign to “shut out the hate and call it out.”
But on Friday, after The Associated Press reported on the planned joint appearance, Stevens released a lengthy statement calling on El-Sayed to condemn an ad by an independent left-wing group that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices.
“Abdul promises to get money out of politics,” Stevens wrote. “He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.”
El-Sayed responded: “So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand.”
He made clear the ad was not made by his campaign and said “I do not agree with the contents of that ad.”
Trump praised Stevens in a Truth Social post, saying she was “a Highly Respected Democrat” and that her support from Black and Jewish voters in Michigan is “virtually unprecedented.”
“Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did,” Trump wrote. “It’s a thing called bravery, and few people have it like just displayed by Congresswoman Haley Stevens!”
Appearing with Trump in Iowa for a campaign rally, House Speaker Mike Johnson said that he spoke to Stevens after she endorsed Rogers. Johnson said he “encouraged her to stay safe and keep speaking the truth.”
A spokesman for the Republican National Committee, Hunter Lovell, said Democrats who feel abandoned by El-Sayed “have a home” with Rogers.
