sources.news_title: Haley Stevens endorses Mike Rogers as El-Sayed rift deepens
sources.text:
Democratic Representative Haley Stevens endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan’s closely watched Senate race Sunday, delivering a sharp late blow to Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed just days before an election that could determine control of the chamber.
The endorsement came after Stevens, who narrowly lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed in August, appeared alongside Rogers at a Detroit church service. Stevens, who had originally backed El-Sayed, had recently been dropped from a planned appearance with him as an escalating dispute over Israel spilled into the campaign's closing stretch.
Michigan is one of the Senate seats Democrats likely cannot afford to lose if they hope to take control of the chamber.
Read More on Politics
Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority and are defending 22 of the 35 seats contested this year. To capture a 51-seat majority, Democrats must hold all 13 of their current seats—including Michigan—and flip four Republican-held seats. A loss in Michigan would force Democrats to win an additional GOP seat elsewhere, significantly narrowing their path to Senate control and bolstering Republicans' efforts to maintain congressional alignment for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s administration.
El-Sayed brushed aside Stevens' endorsement of his opponent on Sunday, telling reporters he remains focused on voters and substantive policy differences.
“At the end of the day, I actually don't think about Haley Stevens,” he said. “I'm just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all.”
El-Sayed argued that voters who support abortion rights, expanded healthcare, infrastructure spending, public education and unions should support his campaign, adding: “The principles that we believe in as Democrats are really quite clear. I stand for all of them.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat, in a series of X posts on Sunday called Stevens’ decision a “despicable betrayal” and said Senate Democrats remained united behind El-Sayed. He condemned Republican attacks on El-Sayed as “racist, Islamophobic” and accused the GOP of “ugly and un-American fearmongering."
Stevens has defended her decision to endorse Rogers, telling reporters, “At some point, you got to look at who's standing for country.” She added that while “90 percent of the votes I'm going to cast are going to be for Democrats,” her Senate vote would go to Rogers.
Rogers praised Stevens and said their alliance was partly about pushing back against antisemitism in Michigan.
“Sometimes the hate grows so loud that it jeopardizes some of our citizens in this state,” Rogers said, pointing to Jewish students who have faced harassment. “We have gone too far.”
Newsweek reached out to the El-Sayed campaign by email Sunday for comment.
Stevens-El-Sayed Rift Explained
The fracture between Stevens and El-Sayed highlights ideological divisions that have shadowed Michigan Democrats since one of the year’s most competitive primary races.
El-Sayed defeated Stevens with 48.4 percent of the vote to 47.6 percent, a difference of fewer than 14,000 votes, according to certified results.
The primary underscored broader rifts within the party as Stevens carried the backing of much of the Democratic establishment, while El-Sayed drew support from prominent national progressives. Foreign policy, particularly U.S. involvement in the Middle East and the war in Gaza, emerged as a primary point of friction.
During an October debate, El-Sayed declined to say whether Iran or Israel posed a greater danger to the United States. After saying, “I don't want to be pushed into war by Israel, and I don't want to be in a war with Iran,” he was pressed to choose which country represented the greater threat. El-Sayed responded: “That's, again, a ridiculous question. I think both of them have proven dangerous in their own way. One, at risk of attacking us. One, getting us into wars we have no business fighting.”
Some Republicans, meanwhile, have repeatedly sought to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood during his campaign, which El-Sayed has denied having any ties to.
Tensions flared again in the final days of the campaign over an independent political action committee's campaign ad linking domestic economic issues to foreign aid. The spot, funded by the pro-El-Sayed Rebellion PAC, showed a couple grocery shopping and talking about putting back a carton of eggs because “we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians,” before criticizing U.S. military assistance to Israel in its war in Gaza.
The Anti-Defamation League labeled the ad a "case study in antisemitism," and Stevens called on El-Sayed to forcefully denounce it. El-Sayed, who did not produce or approve the ad, distanced himself from the PAC’s messaging. Speaking to reporters Saturday, he reiterated that he had no involvement with the spot and declined further comment on the matter.
El-Sayed has rejected suggestions that his criticism of Israel is antisemitic, saying his “commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own kids.”
Meanwhile, Stevens directly criticized El-Sayed’s stance Friday, writing in a statement: "Abdul promises to get money out of politics. He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford."
El-Sayed pushed back, accusing Stevens of "relitigating a primary that ended three months ago."
The dispute took a turn when Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, announced he would support Rogers, citing concerns over El-Sayed’s rhetoric and foreign policy positions.
The escalating row disrupted planned Democratic show-of-unity events on Sunday. Stevens was originally scheduled to appear alongside El-Sayed and Democratic Representative Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. However, Democratic Representative Debbie Dingell of Michigan told The Associated Press she asked Stevens not to attend because the feud had become "way too distracting."
Hours later, Stevens joined Rogers at Perfecting Church in Detroit to deliver her endorsement of the Republican.
Stevens Explains Reason for Switch
Stevens said her decision to endorse Rogers followed her rupture with El-Sayed and reflected concerns about what she characterized as hateful rhetoric.
In a video posted on X announcing the endorsement, Stevens said El-Sayed had made clear that she was no longer welcome in his campaign.
“Abdul said I was no longer welcome in his campaign, and that I should stay away,” the congresswoman said. “And he's right, and that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.”
Stevens also cited streamer Hasan Piker and argued that Michigan voters faced a broader choice about the messages being presented to young people. “What our students see, what our children see, and who we are as Michiganders is not hate, and is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now,” she said.
Stevens stressed that she remained a Democrat, saying she still believed in the positions she had previously taken.
Stevens told reporters on Sunday that her endorsement was “a personal and private decision,” adding, “I’m here with the person who I am voting for for United States Senate, and that is Mike Rogers.”
Rogers said he was “honored” to have earned Stevens’ vote and described the endorsement as being about opposition to hate rather than partisan politics.
“This is more a statement about standing together against hate and the future of this state and this country than it is anything else,” Rogers said.
Rogers said Stevens made one point particularly clear during their conversation: “Remember, I'm still a Democrat.”
Muslim Brotherhood Allegations Against El-Sayed
Some Republicans have repeatedly sought to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, but the claims were made without supporting evidence.
Senator Ted Cruz of Texas raised the allegation during an August Senate Judiciary subcommittee hearing where he connected El-Sayed to the Islamist movement.
Rogers also confronted El-Sayed about alleged Muslim Brotherhood associations during their final debate. El-Sayed denied belonging to the organization and criticized Rogers for invoking his family while advancing the accusation.
“He keeps raising this question about this association with an organization I’ve never been a part of,” El-Sayed said. “It doesn’t make any sense and it’s actually really quite beneath you, Mike.”
Trump recently called El-Sayed a "Muslim radical" and said he was a member of the Islamist organization.
"To the people of Michigan: Mohamed El-Sayed is bad news. He's a Muslim radical. He's a Muslim Brotherhood member, even though he denies it," Trump said in a video posted to Truth Social last month.
The Muslim Brotherhood is an Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928. Some governments have banned the organization or designated it as a terrorist group, but the United States has not designated the Muslim Brotherhood in its entirety as a foreign terrorist organization.
Democrats Condemn Stevens Endorsement
Stevens’ decision to endorse Rogers triggered backlash from Democrats, including members of Stevens’ own staff, who announced resignations while throwing their support behind El-Sayed.
Justin German, Stevens’ chief of staff, wrote in a statement, first shared by CNN, that he and other members of the team resigned following her decision.
“As Haley Stevens’ Chief of Staff for eight years, I speak on behalf of our team in wholeheartedly supporting Abdul El-Sayed for Senate,” the statement said. “We are shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens’ decision to support Mike Rogers.”
German added: “As of this morning, many members of our team have resigned, including myself,” while urging Michigan voters to support El-Sayed and other Democrats.
Curtis Hertel Jr., chair of the Michigan Democratic Party, similarly rejected Stevens’ move, saying the state party remained “united and fully” behind El-Sayed.
“Mike Rogers is Donald Trump’s hand-picked candidate for Senate, a rubber stamp for Trump’s toxic agenda, and a corrupt politician looking out only for himself,” he said in the statement on social media.
Hertel said Stevens had “abandoned everything she claims to care about,” adding that Democrats would not allow “these eleventh-hour distractions” to deter the party.
The criticism also came from national Democrats. Virgie Rollins, chair of the Democratic National Committee’s Black Caucus, said in a statement posted on X Sunday that the caucus was “dismayed” by the endorsement.
“We are dismayed that Congresswoman Haley Stevens has revealed herself to be a sellout who used Black Michiganders for a political stunt,” Rollins said. “Congresswoman Stevens has lost her way, and Michiganders know that Mike Rogers is a shill for Trump.”
Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand also stood behind El-Sayed, saying in a statement posted to X: “The stakes of this election could not be higher: Mike Rogers is a rubber stamp for Donald Trump, and together they plan to continue sowing chaos and making life unaffordable for families while prioritizing their billionaire donors at the expense of Michigan families.”
The congresswoman also faced a hostile response during her appearance with Rogers. In a video posted by independent journalist Aaron Rupar to social media, a protester could be heard shouting, “Haley Stevens is a traitor!”
Former Democratic Representative Susan Wild, a longtime friend and former congressional colleague of Stevens, called the endorsement “appalling” and said it marked a breaking point in their relationship.
Wild said the two entered Congress together in 2018 and had been close personally, recalling Stevens’ support following the death of Wild’s partner. Despite previous disagreements over Israel and American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), Wild said she had avoided publicly challenging Stevens because “her good points outweighed the issues I disagreed with her on.”
“Today, that changes,” Wild wrote. “I’m shocked by Haley’s endorsement. I’m terribly sad and disappointed. I’m furious and will be more so if we lose the MI senate race.”
Wild also predicted lasting consequences for Stevens among congressional Democrats, writing that “she will be a pariah among her friends in the Democratic caucus in Congress.”
What Polls Show in the Michigan Senate Race
Recent polling has generally shown El-Sayed ahead of Rogers, although the size of his advantage varies.
A CNN/SSRS poll conducted October 20 to 27 found El-Sayed leading Rogers 49 percent to 42 percent among likely voters. The survey of 768 likely voters had a margin of error of 4.7 percentage points.
A Marist survey conducted October 15 to 18 showed a considerably closer contest, with El-Sayed at 50 percent and Rogers at 48 percent among likely voters. That two-point difference was within the survey's 4.3-percentage-point margin of error.
An earlier YouGov poll also showed a narrow race, with El-Sayed at 49 percent and Rogers at 48 percent.
The surveys were conducted before Stevens' endorsement of Rogers, meaning they do not measure whether her late defection will affect the race.
What Happens Next
El-Sayed and Rogers are heading into the final stretch of the Michigan Senate race with less than 48 hours until Election Day.

Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan endorsed Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday, Nov. 1, after attending a church service alongside him in Detroit, marking a significant break with her party’s nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, just two days before the midterm elections.
Stevens and Rogers appeared together at Perfecting Church after plans for the congresswoman to campaign alongside El-Sayed and Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., collapsed amid disagreements over political advertising involving Israel and the rising cost of groceries.
Congressional reporter Mychael Schnell of MS NOW reported on X that Stevens was “attending church services” with Rogers, although the two had been spotted arriving separately.
The appearance followed several days of increasingly public disagreements between Stevens and El-Sayed, who narrowly defeated her in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary in August.
Stevens had endorsed El-Sayed shortly after the primary and appeared alongside him at a unity breakfast that month. However, the two had not campaigned together since, despite Democratic efforts to bring them together ahead of Tuesday’s general election.
According to reporting by MS NOW, the latest dispute began when Stevens issued a statement Friday demanding that El-Sayed publicly condemn an advertisement produced by Rebellion PAC, an independent political organization unaffiliated with his campaign.
The advertisement connected rising grocery prices in the United States to American financial and military assistance to Israel, prompting Stevens to accuse the group of promoting antisemitic messaging.
Stevens also criticized El-Sayed’s previous campaign statements concerning Israel, arguing that the advertisement reflected themes he had advanced during the Democratic primary.
She said the outside group “did not invent its argument” and urged El-Sayed to reconsider his approach to discussing Israel in connection with domestic economic issues.
“Abdul promises to get money out of politics,” Stevens wrote. “He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.”
El-Sayed rejected Stevens’ criticism, accusing her of reopening disputes from the Democratic primary rather than concentrating on the general election.
“So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand,” El-Sayed responded.
By Saturday evening, El-Sayed had explicitly distanced himself from the Rebellion PAC advertisement.
“I do not agree with the contents of that ad,” he said, emphasizing that his campaign had not produced or authorized it.
Stevens subsequently welcomed his statement, but the disagreement had already disrupted plans for a joint campaign appearance in Detroit.
Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., who helped arrange the event with Clyburn, said she asked Stevens not to attend because the controversy had become a distraction from the campaign.
“I’m the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting,” Dingell told The Associated Press. “This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank.”
Instead, Stevens attended Perfecting Church with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, while El-Sayed participated in another church service with Democratic officials.
During her appearance, Stevens praised Rogers’ support for investment in Black-owned businesses.
The development quickly escalated beyond the church appearance when Stevens announced her endorsement of Rogers, reversing her previous support for El-Sayed.
“I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today,” Stevens wrote in a statement accompanying a video posted on social media.
The endorsement followed a separate declaration by Stevens’ fiancé, Jason Turkish, who said earlier in the week that he intended to vote for Rogers because of concerns about El-Sayed’s statements involving Israel and the Jewish community.
Stevens had previously maintained that she would support the Democratic nominee despite those disagreements.
Rogers, a former Republican congressman endorsed by President Donald Trump, praised Stevens for speaking publicly about the controversy.
“Representative Haley Stevens is a courageous leader who deserves the respect of every Michigan voter,” Rogers wrote Friday.
He also criticized El-Sayed over the advertisement and his previous statements concerning Israel.
The Associated Press reported Sunday that Stevens’ longtime chief of staff resigned following the development, with additional staff departures expected.
The dispute has exposed disagreements among Michigan Democrats over U.S. policy toward Israel, antisemitism and the party’s efforts to maintain support among Jewish, Black and Arab American voters.
El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, has criticized Israel’s military operations in Gaza and opposed unconditional American military assistance to Israel. Stevens has maintained a more supportive position toward Israel and has argued that some of El-Sayed’s rhetoric risks alienating Jewish voters.
El-Sayed has also faced criticism over campaign appearances involving political commentator Hasan Piker, whose previous statements concerning Israel have generated controversy.
The disagreement carries particular importance because Michigan’s Senate race will determine who succeeds retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.
El-Sayed is attempting to retain the seat for Democrats, while Rogers is seeking to return to Congress as Republicans defend their Senate majority.
Michigan Democrats had planned Sunday’s church appearances as part of a broader effort to encourage turnout in Detroit, where Black voters represent a significant share of the electorate.
El-Sayed continued those appearances alongside Clyburn, Dingell, Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., and other Democratic officials.
During his remarks at church, El-Sayed emphasized the influence of religious communities on his upbringing and public service.
“It’s in churches like this, in pews like the ones in which you sit, that the foundation of my life was built,” he said.
Stevens’ decision to endorse Rogers came after months of tension following the Democratic primary, which included substantial outside spending and disagreements over Israel policy.
Her endorsement also marked a departure from the position she had taken immediately after losing the nomination, when she pledged to support El-Sayed in the general election.
With voting scheduled for Tuesday, Nov. 3, the public disagreement has become a major development in Michigan’s closely contested Senate race, leaving Democratic leaders confronting a last-minute division while Rogers receives support from one of his opponent’s most prominent former primary rivals.

Democrat endorses Republican candidate in key Michigan Senate race as party spat erupts
- Published
A Democrat in Michigan has endorsed the Republican candidate in the state's crucial US Senate contest, as a spat with her own party's candidate Abdul El-Sayed escalated just days before the vote.
Haley Stevens, a sitting congresswoman who lost out on the Democratic Senate nomination to El-Sayed, made a surprise appearance alongside the Republican candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday.
"I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," she said in a video posted to X shortly after that appearance. "Who we are as Michiganders is not hate and is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now."
"That's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers," Stevens said.
The move stunned many of Stevens' fellow Democrats who condemned her decision to break from the party and switch her support just two days before the election.
The public feud between Stevens, a centrist Democrat, and El-Sayed, who represents the party's left-wing, has boiled over in recent days.
Stevens called on El-Sayed to denounce a campaign advert from an outside liberal group that linked US support for Israel with high prices. El-Sayed criticised the advert and said he had nothing to do with its contents.
Stevens had been scheduled to appear at an event with El-Sayed on Sunday in an effort to display party unity, but he reportedly asked her not to come and she chose to attend a church service with his Republican opponent instead.
"This is a very close election, we all know that, but Abdul made clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn't need me there, that he didn't want me there," Stevens told reporters as she stood alongside Rogers outside the church.
When asked about Stevens' endorsement, El-Sayed told reporters he was focused on the problems Michiganders are facing.
"At the end of the day, I don't think about Haley Stevens," he said on Sunday. "None of this matters."
The Michigan Senate race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest in Tuesday's midterm elections. It is one of a handful of battleground contests that will ultimately decide control of the Senate.
The seat is currently held by a retiring Democrat and the last time a Republican was elected to this Senate seat was in 1994. But in presidential elections, it is one of the crucial swing states - Michigan voted for Joe Biden in 2020 but Donald Trump in 2024.
Rogers welcomed Stevens' endorsement and said it showed "courage" during brief remarks with reporters.
President Donald Trump echoed that sentiment, saying on Truth Social that "[Stevens] showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did".
Many of Stevens' staff reportedly resigned immediately after her announcement, while the chair of the Democratic Party in Michigan said her decision "shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about".
"We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum," Curtis Hertel said in a statement.
In downtown Detroit, several Democrats the BBC spoke to said they were disappointed by Stevens' endorsement of Rogers.
"I just genuinely don't understand it," she said. "I do think it's a betrayal of the party because the things she stands for are not the same things that he stands for as a Republican."
"Maybe she had frustrations with the party," Matthew Barera, another Michigan voter, said.
Others, including Republicans who support Rogers, said they doubted it would make a difference to the race.
"People can see right through her actions, you know? She's just angry," Marissa Lee, a Rogers supporter, told the BBC. "She is not going to make anybody change their mind."
Over the weekend, as Stevens' criticism of El-Sayed escalated, a number of Democratic politicians in Michigan publicly encouraged her to end the feud and back the party's candidates more directly.
On Sunday, Democratic Senator Chuck Schumer called Stevens' endorsement of Rogers "a despicable betrayal" of her political party.
After a bruising and sometimes bitter campaign earlier this year, El-Sayed, a left-wing outsider, defeated Stevens, the establishment-backed congresswoman, to win the party's nomination for the US Senate race.
The primary, and the pair's subsequent feud, has underlined divisions over the party's direction ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
Former public health official El-Sayed, who is the son of Egyptian immigrants, has channelled grassroots frustration with Washington politics as well as US ties to Israel.
Stevens is a more centrist Democrat - and had the support of party figures such as Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer during the primary race.
The party is hoping to regain control of the Senate in Tuesday's elections, but will need a net gain of four seats to do so. A loss in Michigan - which they currently hold - would represent a major blow and leave them needing to flip five seats.

Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Michigan GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers amid rift with Abdul El-Sayed
Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday amid a rift with Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed that has come front and center in the final sprint to Election Day.
"Our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away, and he's right," Stevens said in a video posted on social media Sunday. "And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today."
Stevens appeared alongside Rogers at a Detroit church on Sunday.
Stevens, who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in Michigan's Democratic primary in August, where she was heavily supported by the Senate Democrats' campaign arm, called on El-Sayed last week to condemn an outside group's ad linking U.S. military aid to Israel to rising grocery prices, which she characterized as antisemitic. El-Sayed accused Stevens of "relitigating a primary that ended three months ago," although he has also clarified that the ad "was not made by me" and said he disagrees with its contents.
El-Sayed pushed to return the attention to the issues facing Michigan voters as he takes on the GOP candidate, Rogers. But Rogers praised Stevens on Friday for calling on El-Sayed to denounce the ad, and for expressing concerns raised by Michigan Jewish voters.
"Representative Haley Stevens is a courageous leader who deserves the respect of every Michigan voter," Rogers said in a post on X. "She has conducted herself with nothing but class since the Democratic primary, a primary where a majority of voters did not vote for her party's nominee."
Speaking to reporters after he appeared with Stevens at the Detroit church Sunday, Rogers said he was honored to receive her support.
"This is more a statement about standing together against hate and the future of this state and this country than it is anything else," Rogers said.
Rogers said he got the call Sunday morning from Stevens, and the two decided to appear together at the church. He said he and Stevens talked about what was better for the future of the state. And he noted that Stevens reminded him at the end of their call that she remains a Democrat.
Responding to the endorsement on Sunday, El-Sayed said, "I actually don't think about Haley Stevens."
"This is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from their government. I'm a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not the ones who are talking about."
Stevens said she's "not trying to harm" the Democratic Party with the move, insisting that she isn't "turning her back on Democrats."
"It is this one vote," she said. "And I will tell you why: Because when you see hate, when you see us standing with Hasan Piker, and repeated hate, it's not acceptable."
"That's it. It's my personal and private decision," Stevens said. "It's a Michigan moment, and everyone is entitled to their opinion."
Stevens said she "meant it" when she previously endorsed El-Sayed. But she added, "He chose to close his campaign by saying I wasn't welcome."
The appearance with Rogers came after Stevens had been expected to appear with El-Sayed at a unity event Sunday alongside Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. But El-Sayed said Saturday, "I would rather not distract from the key issues of this campaign."
Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, said last week that he is voting for Rogers.
Democrats stunned by reversal, Trump praises Stevens
After Stevens endorsed Rogers, top Democrats expressed their continued support for El-Sayed's candidacy, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.
"Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors," Schumer said in a statement.
In a post on X, Schumer called it a "despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens."
Democratic Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan said Michiganders "want leaders focused on making their lives more affordable."
"That's what they're talking about, not Congresswoman Stevens' continued efforts to get attention," she said in a statement. " If we are going to fight to improve the lives of working men and women in Michigan, we must stay focused on electing Democrats up and down the ballot, and that includes electing Abdul El-Sayed as Michigan's next senator."
Michigan Democratic Party chair Curtis Hertel posted on social media that Stevens is "not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future."
President Trump praised Stevens for backing Rogers.
"Her following is huge, and the level of respect from the People of Michigan, especially our African American and Jewish populations, is virtually unparalleled," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did."
He told reporters later: "That was a big move, I think. Nobody expected that, but it's a smart thing to do because El-Sayed would destroy our country. So I thought that was fantastic."
Appearing with Mr. Trump in Iowa for a campaign rally, House Speaker Mike Johnson said he spoke to Stevens after she endorsed Rogers and "encouraged her to stay safe and keep speaking the truth."
More broadly, Republicans cited the move as they billed El-Sayed as too liberal for the state.
"Democrats who feel Abdul has abandoned them have a home with Mike, who is building a winning coalition of Democrats, Independents, and Republicans to save Michigan from El-Sayed's radical, terrorist-sympathizing agenda," Republican National Committee spokesman Hunter Lovell said in a statement. "The center of Michigan politics has moved, and Abdul is on the wrong side of it."
Stevens' team resigns after endorsement
Ahead of Stevens' endorsement of Rogers and her appearance on Sunday, her longtime chief of staff resigned, with a number of staff members expected to follow soon.
In a statement first shared by CNN, Stevens' former chief of staff Justin German said he and the team are "shocked and heartbroken" by her decision to support Rogers and that they are "wholeheartedly supporting" El-Sayed for Senate.
"This election is too important to sow division or stand on the sidelines," German wrote. "Those of us who are Michigan voters are supporting Democrats up and down the ballot and have been working all season to elect strong Democratic majorities to the House and Senate — we will continue to do so."
"Hello, as of November 1st I am no longer with the Office of Congresswoman Haley Stevens," an automated email reply from Stevens' former communications director, Logan Basch, reads.
Joetta Appiah, Stevens' former press secretary and campaign spokesperson, said in a statement that Stevens is "walking back on everything her campaign stood for."
"Michiganders deserve better, and they need to stay focused on what matters, which is electing Abdul to the Senate to stand up to Donald Trump, hold his administration accountable, and fight to lower costs for Michiganders," Appiah said. "We cannot let this distract us from Tuesday."
60 MINUTES will feature Ross Douthat's exclusive interviews with Michigan Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers.

By JOEY CAPPELLETTI, COREY WILLIAMS and MIKE HOUSEHOLDER
DETROIT (AP) — Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers as Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill.
Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary.
“Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. “And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.”
El-Sayed dismissed the endorsement when asked about it by reporters later Sunday, saying he’s focused on issues voters care about, such as the high cost of living.
“At the end of the day I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he said, adding later: “None of this matters.”
Michigan Democratic leaders were left shocked. With just less than 48 hours to go before Election Day, a party that had spent months trying to unite behind its Senate nominee was suddenly grappling with an extraordinary defection in one of this year’s most important races.
Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. He has also been criticized by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker.
El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is facing Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by the retiring Democrat, Gary Peters. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party’s effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump’s second term.
Stevens and El-Sayed were originally scheduled to attend church together, along with other Michigan and national Democrats, including South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. Democrats hoped it would be a show of unity as they worked to boost turnout in the Detroit area, where concerns have lingered about enthusiasm among Black and Jewish voters in key Democratic strongholds.
Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded.
Stevens’ team resigns as Democrats are stunned by reversal
After the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and her fiance Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, “I’m not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote.”

It also led her longtime chief of staff to resign, with a number of staff members expected to follow soon, according to a person familiar with the developments who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters.
“We are shocked and heartbroken,” the aide said in a statement.

Hertel later wrote that Stevens “is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.”
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, who supported Stevens in the primary, denounced her endorsement of Rogers.
“This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens,” Schumer wrote in a social media post.
Dingell says she disinvited Stevens after it became ‘distracting’
Among the Democrats who joined El-Sayed at church Sunday morning were U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan, U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Senate primary before voting began.
Dingell, a senior Democratic figure in the state who helped organize the planned joint appearance, said she asked Stevens not to attend and that Stevens told her she would abide by that.
“I’m the one who pulled it, because it had become way too distracting,” Dingell said in an interview before Stevens appeared with Rogers. “This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank.”
In the August primary, Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighboring Oakland County, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters who are important parts of the Democratic coalition.
Early voting for Tuesday’s election has been underway since Oct. 24. As of Friday, more than 1.8 million people had already voted in Michigan.
How did we get here?
The Democratic primary was among the most bitter this year. Each candidate accused the other of making personal attacks. Tens of millions of dollars in outside spending poured into the race, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s affiliated super PAC, which backed Stevens. El-Sayed took particular offense to an outside group’s ad accusing him of disrespecting women.

But on Friday, after The Associated Press reported on the planned joint appearance, Stevens released a lengthy statement calling on El-Sayed to condemn an ad by an independent left-wing group that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices.
